content: In patients with impaired renal function, the clearance of both amoxicillin and clavulanate is reduced due to decreased renal clearance. Both amoxicillin and clavulanate can be effectively removed from the circulation through hemodialysis. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a combination of a semi-synthetic antibiotic, amoxicillin, and a β-lactamase inhibitor, clavulanate potassium (the potassium salt of clavulanic acid). Amoxicillin is a derivative of ampicillin, based on the penicillin nucleus, 6-aminopenicillanic acid. Its molecular formula is C16H19N3O5S·3H2O, with a molecular weight of 419.46. Chemically, amoxicillin is (2S,5R,6R)-6-[3,3-dimethyl-7-oxo-4-thia-1-azabicyclo[3.2.0]heptane-2-carboxylic acid] trihydrate. Clavulanic acid is produced by the fermentation of Streptomyces clavuligerus. It is a β-lactam structurally related to penicillins and has the ability to inactivate a wide range of β-lactamases by blocking their active sites. Clavulanic acid is particularly effective against clinically significant plasmid-mediated β-lactamases, which are often responsible for transferred drug resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins. The molecular formula of clavulanate potassium is C8H8KNO5, with a molecular weight of 237.25. Chemically, it is potassium (Z)-(2R,5R)-3-(2-hydroxyethylidene)-7-oxo-4-oxa-1-azabicyclo[3.2.0]heptane-2-carboxylate. Each 5 mL of reconstituted amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium oral suspension (600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL) contains 600 mg of amoxicillin as the trihydrate and 42.9 mg of clavulanic acid as the potassium salt. The potassium content per 5 mL is 0.23 mEq (equivalent to 9 mg). The dry powder appears as a white to yellowish-white crystalline powder, and the suspension is almost white to yellow, forming a homogeneous mixture. Inactive ingredients in the powder for oral suspension include caramel flavor, carboxymethyl cellulose sodium, citric acid, colloidal silicon dioxide, microcrystalline cellulose, orange flavor, raspberry flavor, saccharin sodium, silicon dioxide, sodium citrate, and xanthan gum. The pharmacokinetics of amoxicillin and clavulanate were studied in 19 pediatric patients (aged 8 months to 11 years) who received amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium oral suspension (600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL) at an amoxicillin dose of 45 mg/kg every 12 hours with food. Approximately 50% to 70% of amoxicillin and 25% to 40% of clavulanic acid are excreted unchanged in the urine within the first 6 hours after administration of 10 mL of the 250 mg/62.5 mg per 5 mL suspension. Probenecid delays the excretion of amoxicillin but does not affect the renal excretion of clavulanic acid. Neither component is highly protein-bound; clavulanic acid is approximately 25% bound to human serum proteins, while amoxicillin is about 18% bound. Amoxicillin diffuses readily into most body tissues and fluids, except for the brain and spinal fluid. Clavulanic acid, like amoxicillin, is well-distributed in body tissues, as demonstrated in animal studies. Amoxicillin is a semi-synthetic antibiotic with broad-spectrum bactericidal activity against many gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms. However, it is susceptible to degradation by β-lactamases, which limits its activity against organisms that produce these enzymes. Clavulanic acid, a β-lactam structurally related to penicillin, inactivates a wide range of β-lactamase enzymes commonly found in microorganisms resistant to penicillins and cephalosporins. It is particularly effective against clinically significant plasmid-mediated β-lactamases responsible for transferred drug resistance. The clavulanic acid component of amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium protects amoxicillin from degradation by β-lactamase enzymes, effectively extending the antibiotic spectrum of amoxicillin to include many bacteria that are normally resistant to amoxicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics. This combination possesses the distinctive properties of a broad-spectrum antibiotic and a β-lactamase inhibitor. Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid has demonstrated activity against most isolates of Streptococcus pneumoniae (including isolates with penicillin MICs ≤ 2 mcg/mL), Haemophilus influenzae (including β-lactamase–producing isolates), and Moraxella catarrhalis (including β-lactamase–producing isolates). However, the safety and efficacy of amoxicillin/clavulanic acid in treating infections caused by these microorganisms have not been established in adequate and well-controlled clinical trials. Staphylococcus aureus (including β-lactamase–producing isolates) is also susceptible to this combination. However, staphylococci resistant to methicillin/oxacillin must be considered resistant to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. Streptococcus pyogenes does not produce β-lactamase and is therefore susceptible to amoxicillin alone. Clinical trials have established the effectiveness of amoxicillin alone in treating certain infections caused by S. pyogenes. When available, clinical microbiology laboratories should provide cumulative results of in vitro susceptibility tests for antimicrobial drugs used in local hospitals and practice areas. These reports should guide physicians in selecting the most effective antimicrobial agents. Quantitative methods, such as determining minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs), should be used to estimate bacterial susceptibility to antimicrobial compounds. These MICs should be determined using standardized procedures.
